title: Pride and humility
hook: pride, the root sin, is cured by humility, seeing yourself truly

segments.voice: Yesterday, temperance: honey at the right measure, good things kept as gifts. Your line was enough is joy. What did you stop at enough? Day one thousand two hundred one.

Naaman is a great general, honored by his king, and he has leprosy. A captive girl from Israel, a servant in his house, tells his wife there's a prophet back home who could heal him. So Naaman arrives at Elisha's door with horses and chariots and gifts. Elisha doesn't even come out. He sends a messenger: go wash in the Jordan. And Naaman storms off in a rage. He expected the prophet to come out, call on God, wave a hand over the spot. Our rivers back home are better than that one, he says. He's about to go home unhealed, because the cure was too ordinary for him. Today: pride, and its cure.

Then his servants step in, and what they say is the whole lesson in one sentence: "My father, if the prophet had bid thee do some great thing, wouldest thou not have done it? how much rather then, when he saith to thee, Wash, and be clean?" Naaman listens. He goes down to the river, does exactly as he was told, and his skin comes back like a little child's. Notice who rescued him from his pride: a captive girl and his own servants. The people he least expected to need. Some Christian teachers treat pride as the root of the other sins. The Book of Sirach, in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles and among the King James Apocrypha, puts it plainly: "pride is the beginning of sin." And Proverbs adds where it leads: "Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall." But here's what's easy to get wrong. The cure isn't thinking you're worthless. Paul tells the Romans "not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think; but to think soberly." Soberly. Accurately. Not higher than the truth, and not lower either. Humility, in this picture, is simply seeing yourself truly: gifted and limited, capable and in need of help. Pride can't ask for help, because asking admits a limit. Humility asks easily. The letter of James puts it in one line: "God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble." Some readers hear Naaman in it: the gift was there all along, waiting for him to stoop to the river.

Here's the practice: find something you need help with. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you've been struggling with alone because asking felt like admitting something: a task at work, a repair, a skill, a heavy week. Name it honestly. Then name one person who could help, maybe someone you wouldn't expect, like Naaman's servants. Picture asking them, in plain words. If you pray, you can ask God for help too. The bell holds the time.
Pride and humility. Pride, which some Christian teachers call the root of sin, thinks higher of itself than the truth. Humility sees itself truly, and so it can ask for help.
Your line: see yourself truly. Today, ask the person you named for help with the thing you named, in a sentence or two, without apologizing for asking. Day one thousand two hundred one.

howItsDone: Some Christian traditions name pride among the deadly sins and humility as its remedy, and practice humility through confession, accepting correction and help, and serving others.

original.note: Greek: lowliness of mind, humility; the word in Philippians 2:3.

trapdoor: what you thought: humility means putting yourself down.
what it means: seeing yourself truly, gifts and limits both, which frees you to ask for help.
what a scholar hears: Romans 12:3 doesn't say think less of yourself; it says don't think more highly than you ought, but soberly.
